---
title: "Flow Matching"
---
The flow matching transformer model is a flexible and stochastic surrogate.


## When this might be a good fit

The flow matching surrogate is a good option when stochasticity is needed. Architecturally, it is implemented as a modified transformer and also supports static and sequence conditioning.

## How flow matching works

### Architecture
The flow matching surrogate is parametrised with a *non-causal* transformer that processes the entire sequence in parallel.

### Flow Matching

Flow Matching and Diffusion models are the current state-of-the-art learning algorithms for continuous valued data (e.g. images, protein-structure prediction). In brief, these models learn time-varying velocity fields which can be used to transport a sample of pure noise (e.g. from a Gaussian) to the data distribution. In order to generate samples the time-varying velocity field $v_{\theta}$ must be integrated over time $t$ to transport a noise sample $x_0$ to the data distribution:
$$
x_{\mathrm{pred}} = x_0+\int_{t=0}^{t=1}v_{\theta}(x_t|c)dt\text{, where } c \text{ is conditioning (i.e. surrogate inputs)}
$$


In practice this is achieved via numerical ODE solvers like Euler or Heun, with the number of solver steps introducing a trade-off between speed and quality.

:::{.callout-note  title="Technical note" collapse="true"}
Diffusion models have equivalent ODE and SDE forms and can be sampled via SDE-solvers like Euler-Maruyama or ODE-solvers like Heun. See @song2021scorebased.
:::

By fixing the conditioning $c$ and varying the initial noise, you can sample multiple realisations rather than the average realisation that an MLP or Autoregressive transformer learn.

:::{.callout-tip}
The mathematical details of these models and the derivation of their training objectives are out of scope but if you're interested you may find these resources helpful:

* [Accessible introduction to Diffusion (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iv-5mZ_9CPY)
* [Introduction to Normalising Flows and Flow Matching (Blog)](https://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/blog/2024/01/20/flow-matching.html)
* [Explanation of score-based diffusion by its inventor (Blog)](https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/#connection-to-diffusion-models-and-others)
* [Unifying flow matching and diffusion (Monograph)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.21890)

:::


## Configuring a Flow Matching model

The installed preset is `model=flow_matching`: `n_blocks=2`, `n_head=4`,
`n_kv_head=4`, `embd_dim=64`, `cond_dropout_prob=0`, `interpolant=linear`.
Architecture options are flat under `model.model_options`; there is no nested
`sit` configuration. Blocks control depth, embedding width controls capacity,
and head counts control the attention decomposition.

```bash
uv run metis train model=flow_matching model.model_options.embd_dim=128 evaluation.num_steps=100
```

`interpolant=linear` uses linear noise-to-data paths; `trig` selects the
trigonometric interpolant. Both change the training objective/path and should be
recorded with results. `num_steps` and `solver` are sampling options, separate
from training: `model.sample(inputs, n_samples=100, num_steps=50, solver="heun")`.
Euler and Heun are supported. More integration steps cost time and do not by
themselves establish predictive calibration.

Dimensions come from the dataset. `qkv_bias` and `in_and_out_biases` are optional
architecture fields. For observed channels use
`model.observed_outputs=[intervention]`; the full supplied path is available to
the network. This is conditional generation, not a causal forecast. See
[conditioning](../package/conditioning.qmd). Classifier-free guidance is not a
public sampling feature; do not interpret conditioning dropout as such a guarantee.
